title: The Brahmanas' Wives Bring Food to Krishna
story:
The cowherd boys came back empty-handed. Krishna had sent them across the fields to the brahmanas — learned men performing a sacrifice near Vrindavan — to ask for food in his name and Balarama's, and the brahmanas had given them nothing: no yes, no no, only the murmur of their rites going on without them. When the boys told Krishna this, Krishna only laughed. There was no anger in it. He did not scold the men, and he did not repeat the request. "Go to their wives," he said, "and tell them that I have come, with Balarama."

So the boys went a second time, now to the women's quarters of those same houses. There the wives sat, well-adorned in their own homes, going about the quiet work of the afternoon. The boys bowed to them and spoke with the same respect as before. "Obeisance to you, wives of the brahmanas," they said. "Listen to our words. While pasturing the cows with the cowherds, he has come from far away, with Balarama — and he is hungry."

The wives heard the name, and everything in them rose at once. They had always longed for the sight of Krishna — a longing they carried every day without speaking it aloud. They had heard of him, the dark boy of Vrindavan whose name was on everyone's lips, and they had kept that longing lit like a lamp in a dark room. Now, without a word of hesitation, they filled their vessels with food — food of four kinds, rich and fine, prepared with care — and hurried out toward him. There was something of a festival in that sudden movement: doors flung open, feet hurrying, voices rising, as though the whole women's quarter had been waiting all along for exactly this summons.

Their husbands tried to stop them. Their brothers tried, their kinsmen tried, their own sons called after them from the doorways, asking where they thought they were going and before whom. They called it madness, or worse; they reminded the women of their duties, their good names, the scandal of it. But the women did not slow. A longing kept secret for years has a force that reproach cannot match, and not one of them turned back. They went as rivers run to the sea, drawn by a pull that nothing in the house could answer.

What they left behind was not small: houses, husbands, the good opinion of their kin, the settled shape of a whole life — and they left it all without a backward look. There is no heaviness in the telling of it, only eagerness. They were going to meet the one they had wanted for so long without daring to ask, and their feet seemed to know the way, as though they had walked it a thousand times in their thoughts.

So through the groves of Vrindavan they went, their vessels bright in their hands, their veils and bracelets catching the afternoon light, their faces all turned one way — toward the place where Krishna waited with Balarama and the boys and the grazing cows. Some carried the food balanced high; others held it close against them, as though afraid the afternoon might end before they arrived.

It had taken the men an afternoon of silence to answer him. It took their wives no more than a breath.
reflection: The contrast is the point of the story. The learned brahmanas saw only a herd-boy and sent him away; their wives, who had no learning to lean on and only longing to go by, saw what the longing had prepared them to see. They drop everything — home, kin, reputation — because the one they have wanted is finally near.
next_story_tease: But when the wives reached him, they would refuse to go back at all.
hero_scene: The brahmana wives hurrying through the groves of Vrindavan with bright vessels of food in their hands, their husbands and kinsmen calling them back in vain, their faces turned toward the place where Krishna and Balarama wait with the grazing cows.
